title: Attend to farm business management activities

lessons.title: Preparing budgets for the dairy
lessons.html:
From knowledge to practice

In this practical module you will prepare and use real budgets, analyse financial results and support business decisions on a dairy. Work with the farm's own figures where the owner permits, keeping them confidential.

Step 1: gather data

  • Herd budget: cows in milk by month, culls, heifer sales.
  • Production forecast: litres per cow per day times cows in milk.
  • Milk price forecast including expected component and quality payments.
  • Input prices: feed, fertiliser, fuel, electricity, wages, animal health.
  • Fixed costs from last year's accounts, adjusted for known changes.

Step 2: enterprise budget

ItemPer month (R)
Milk income (420 cows × 21 L × 30 days × R7.40)1 958 040
Cull and calf sales70 000
Gross income2 028 040
Feed1 050 000
Animal health, AI85 000
Parlour, electricity, fuel120 000
Pasture inputs140 000
Total variable costs1 395 000
Gross margin633 040

Step 3: cash flow budget

Spread income and expenses over 12 months according to when cash actually moves: milk paid the month after delivery, fertiliser bought in autumn, annual insurance in one payment, loan repayments on set dates. Calculate the opening balance, net flow and closing balance for each month. Identify months that need overdraft and discuss facilities with the bank in advance.

Step 4: sensitivity

Recalculate the gross margin with milk price 10% lower and feed 10% higher. In the example, income falls by about R196 000 and feed rises by R105 000, cutting the gross margin by about R301 000 to around R332 000. This shows how exposed the farm is.

lessons.title: Monitoring actual performance
lessons.html:
Budget versus actual

Each month compare actual income and costs with the budget. Calculate the variance (actual minus budget) and investigate significant variances.

ItemBudgetActualVariance
Milk incomeR1 958 040R1 870 000−R88 040
FeedR1 050 000R1 120 000+R70 000 (over)

Ask why. Lower milk income could be lower yield, fewer cows in milk, lower price or quality penalties. Higher feed cost could be price increases, higher intake, waste or more bought feed due to poor pasture growth. Each cause needs a different response.

Key operational ratios

  • Feed cost per litre = feed cost ÷ litres sold.
  • Margin over feed cost per cow per day = (milk income − feed cost) ÷ cow days.
  • Labour cost per litre.
  • Total cost per litre compared with milk price: the basic test of profitability.

Bookkeeping tasks

  • Code invoices to the correct cost centres (dairy, young stock, pasture, overheads).
  • Reconcile the milk statement with collection records.
  • Reconcile bank statements monthly.
  • Check payroll inputs: hours, overtime, leave, deductions, UIF.
  • Keep supporting documents for tax and audits.

Asset register

Maintain a register of machinery, equipment and buildings with purchase date, cost and depreciation. Combine with a livestock valuation to prepare the balance sheet. Monitor the debt ratio and current ratio to check solvency and liquidity.

Reporting

Prepare a short monthly management report for the owner: key physical results (litres, SCC, calvings), financial results versus budget, cash position, main variances with explanations, and recommended actions.

Explain variances in plain language in your report. For example: feed cost was R70 000 over budget because the maize price rose and pasture growth was poor in a dry month, so more silage was fed.

lessons.title: Supporting business decisions
lessons.html:
Evaluating a proposal with a partial budget

Proposal: buy a second-hand mixer wagon for R480 000 instead of paying a contractor to mix feed.

Effects on profit per yearR
Reduced costs: contractor fees saved+180 000
Additional income: better intake, estimated+60 000
Additional costs: depreciation (R480 000 over 8 years)−60 000
Additional costs: fuel, repairs, operator time−95 000
Additional costs: interest on capital (approx.)−48 000
Net change in profit+37 000

The proposal appears profitable but the margin is modest and depends on the uncertain intake benefit. Without it, the result would be −R23 000. The manager should present both results and the risks to the owner.

Labour management activities

  • Prepare job descriptions and organograms.
  • Plan recruitment, contracts and induction.
  • Keep employment records and comply with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997, the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 and the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998.
  • Plan training and skills development.

Compliance calendar

Maintain a calendar of statutory and contractual deadlines: tax and UIF submissions, insurance renewals, water use authorisation conditions under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, OHS Act 85 of 1993 requirements, vehicle licences and buyer audits.

Risk management

Review insurance cover for buildings, machinery, livestock and liability. Maintain feed reserves and cash buffers. Diversify income where it makes sense. Document a business continuity plan for power failure, disease outbreak and loss of key staff.

Key points

  • Build enterprise and cash flow budgets from herd and production forecasts.
  • Test budgets for lower milk prices and higher feed prices.
  • Compare actual with budget monthly and explain variances.
  • Use partial budgets and present risks for investment decisions.
  • Keep labour, compliance and risk management activities up to date.
